name: Melatonin
meta: Prescription medicine in India (Schedule H for tablet formulations; verify current
sections: Pale yellow/white crystalline powder; melting point 117 °C.

Discovered in 1958 by Aaron Lerner; use for circadian rhythm disorders patented in 1987 (Monash University) and as a sleep aid in 1995 (MIT). First approval/introduction: Prolonged-release melatonin EU 2007 (Neurim Pharmaceuticals).

Endogenous pineal hormone that acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, promoting sleep onset and re-synchronising circadian rhythm. Receptor / target profile: Agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, regulating the circadian clock and sleep–wake cycle.
Summary: Rapidly absorbed; bioavailability ~15% (first-pass). Tmax ~1 h. Metabolised by CYP1A2 to 6-hydroxymelatonin. Half-life 40–60 min (immediate release).
Circadian rhythm sleep disorders – jet lag, delayed sleep phase
Sleep disturbance in children with ADHD/autism (specialist use)
Jet lag: 3–5 mg at local bedtime for 2–5 days
Doses up to 10 mg used in specialist settings
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Not recommended in hepatic impairment (reduced clearance).
Used at specialist level for sleep disorders in ADHD/autism.

Take after food, 1–2 hours before bedtime; avoid alcohol.
Drowsiness; supportive care. Clearance within ~12 h.
Ferracioli-Oda et al., PLoS One 2013 – meta-analysis: melatonin reduced sleep latency by ~7 minutes and increased total sleep time.
Prolonged-release melatonin trials in adults ≥55 years improved sleep quality and morning alertness.
Take at the same time every night
Avoid bright screens before sleep for best effect
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
